title: Budget Deficits and the National Debt
short: A deficit is one year's shortfall; the debt is the running total of past deficits minus surpluses.
trouble: Students use deficit and debt as the same word, or think a shrinking deficit means the debt is falling.

blocks.html: When Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy spends more than it collects, the government borrows the difference. Two words describe this, and they are easy to mix up: one measures a year, the other the total.

The budget deficit is one year's shortfall: spending (purchases, transfers and interest) minus revenue. A surplus is the reverse. The national debt is the total amount the government owes: the running sum of past deficits minus past surpluses. The deficit is a flow; the debt is a stock.

Think of a bathtub. The water level is the debt; the water pouring in each year is the deficit. As long as water flows in, the level rises, even if the faucet is turned down. A smaller deficit means the debt grows more slowly, not that it falls. The level goes down only when water drains out: a surplus. Economists often compare the debt with GDP, because a larger economy can carry a larger debt.

blocks.name: macro-debt
blocks.cap: Bars: each year's budget balance (red deficits, green surpluses). Line: the debt. Drag a bar, or pick a year and use the slider. The deficits shrink every year, yet the debt keeps rising until the first surplus.

blocks.title: Deficits into debt
blocks.q: The debt starts at \$8,000 billion. Deficits are \$500 billion, then \$300 billion; then there is a \$100 billion surplus. What is the debt after three years?
steps: Add the deficits and subtract the surplus.

blocks.title: Shrinking deficit, growing debt
blocks.q: Last year's deficit was \$700 billion; this year's is \$400 billion. What happened to the debt this year?
steps: There was still a shortfall of \$400 billion, which the government borrowed.
The debt rose by \$400 billion, more slowly than last year, but it rose.

blocks.title: Debt compared with GDP
blocks.q: The debt is \$24,000 billion and GDP is \$30,000 billion. Find the debt-to-GDP ratio.
steps: If GDP grows faster than the debt, this ratio can fall even while the debt rises.

blocks.html: Using deficit and debt as the same word, or thinking a shrinking deficit means the debt is falling. Check: is there still a shortfall this year? Then the debt is still rising.
